findings.passage: and then explained the act as protection rather than as rage or proof of toughness.
findings.problem: Context-fidelity error that removes adverse evidence. In the opened Oprah transcript (S1), Oprah asks whether his father's leaving turned him into 'the kind of angry kid who would end up shooting his brother?' and he answers 'Yes—and my brother was dealing with a lot of demons,' then adds 'I felt like I needed to protect everybody.' He affirms anger first and adds protection; he does not offer protection 'rather than' rage. The same interview opens with 'Anger' at 11 and 'I was angry' about wanting to shoot back. The draft quotes the 'Yes' and then tells the reader it means the opposite. This is the attractive causal story (protection, not rage) overriding his own words, and it props up the Eight thesis at the point where an anger/reactivity reading is just as available.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence states that he agreed the shooting came from anger and also framed it as protecting the family, with no 'rather than as rage' contrast; C28's inference is updated to match; any later passage relying on 'protection, not rage' (e.g. 'What separates them') is consistent with that.

findings.passage: A Three can be ruthless about ownership and can feud, but the reasons Jay-Z gives each time are protection and control, not how it will look.
findings.problem: The discriminator's 'each time' is contradicted by sources the draft itself uses. At the 2019 press conference (S7, opened via theGrio) his stated objection to Travis Scott was rank and billing: 'My problem is (Travis) had the biggest year to me last year, and he's playing on a stage that had an M on it. I didn't see any reason for him to play second fiddle.' He also said 'the process could have been more definite.' The draft keeps 'second fiddle' in the opening but never tests it as Three evidence. His Grammy complaint was explicitly about accolades ('even by your own metrics') and closed on being called 'the greatest of all time.' Billing, rank and recognition are stated reasons about how things look. The test as written is not falsifiable against the record it cites.
findings.acceptance_test: Either 'each time' is replaced by an honest count (which stated reasons are protection/control, and which are rank or recognition), or the 'second fiddle'/'stage that had an M on it' reason and the 'your own metrics' complaint are put in the Type 3 case and answered by a specific, sourced counter-observation. The FAQ and type answer are consistent with the result.

findings.passage: He never describes it as a way to keep performing or to keep winning.
findings.problem: An absolute the draft's own evidence undercuts. On Fresh Air (S2), quoted later in the draft, he describes hiding fear behind armor in order to perform: 'that bravado is an act of, I am so nervous right now, and I'm scared to death. I'm going to act so tough that I'm going to hide it.' He also says his dealing became 'beyond survival. I was successful... I had become addicted to the lifestyle.' Hiding a feeling behind toughness so the show goes on is the Three mechanism the draft says he 'never' describes. The 'wall' and the 'bravado' are not identical, but the reader is not told why one counts and the other does not. Test 1 of 'What separates them' rests on this sentence.
findings.acceptance_test: The 'never' claim is narrowed to what the three wall quotes actually say, and the bravado-as-cover quote is addressed in the first discriminator test (why it does or does not count as suspending feeling to perform), not only listed in the Type 3 section.

findings.passage: Those traits sound more like a withdrawn type, a Nine or a Five, than like the confrontational Eight of the textbook.
findings.problem: The draft tests 3, 9 and 5 but never tests a counterphobic Six, which fits much of the evidence it treats as Eight. The draft's own discriminator for the wall is 'protection against being let down' by a trusted authority (the father as 'superhero' who 'lets you down') and against 'danger' ('survival mode'). That is security and trust language, not specifically control. Its other key material is also Six-shaped: toughness as a front for fear ('I'm scared to death. I'm going to act so tough'), 'I was terrified,' a loyalty code ('it was here in the projects that I learned loyalty'), turning down a deal out of loyalty to Jaz-O, and lines drawn when an ally betrays the group (Kanye bringing family in, the friend who shot at him). As written, the main discriminator does not separate Eight from counterphobic Six, so 'medium confidence' in Eight is not earned against the strongest rival.
findings.acceptance_test: The article includes a short, evidence-based test of counterphobic Six and names a sourced observation that separates Eight from Six (for example, how he relates to authority and institutions once he has power, or whether he seeks or rejects guidance and backing). Otherwise the confidence and the 'strongest alternative' claim are revised. type_hypothesis.alternative_case/discriminator mention the Six test.

findings.passage: The second test is what he does when protecting what is his has a price.
findings.problem: The 'costly choices' are mostly asserted, not shown. Getting his masters back was a negotiated condition of taking a powerful, lucrative job (S9), a win rather than a visible price, and the only cost on record is Dash's claim about their friendship. The Grammy remark was softened with 'we love y'all' and cost nothing documented. Turning down the halftime show ended in a better deal (his company produces the show). The criterion is also applied unevenly. The type answer and FAQ say 'when guarding his family or his work cost him approval, he usually guarded,' but the clearest case on record of him accepting public disapproval for a position of power, the 2019 NFL deal, is counted only as Three evidence. Under the draft's own test it would partly favor Eight. A skeptical reader sees the test bend toward the conclusion in both directions.
findings.acceptance_test: Each example in test 2 names the concrete price he paid, with a source, or it is dropped or reframed as 'terms' rather than 'cost.' The article applies one criterion to the NFL deal and to the Eight examples alike. The 'cost him approval' wording in the type answer and FAQ is either backed by a sourced instance or removed.

findings.passage: His account still matches Jay-Z's own word for his younger self, "cold," and it matches the pattern: when control of the work was at stake, the friendship did not decide the outcome.
findings.problem: Hostile testimony is bent to fit the thesis. In the opened Okayplayer piece (S13), Dash's stated motive is money ('betrayed you for money'), and he calls it an industry norm ('That's the algorithm... divide and conquer, that's a normal story'). He says nothing about control of the work. The masters condition comes from Jay-Z's 2023 account (S9), not from Dash. Matching Dash's insult 'cold' to a 40-year-old describing his 11-year-old self as 'really quiet and really cold' is a word coincidence presented as corroboration. Taken at face value, Dash's account points toward a money, pragmatism or Three reading, not toward Eight. Also, 'He has given other reasons for the split over the years' is not supported by the cited Okayplayer article.
findings.acceptance_test: The paragraph reports Dash's stated motive (money, industry pattern) accurately and acknowledges which reading it favors. The 'cold' match is removed or explicitly labeled as a coincidence of wording, not corroboration. The 'other reasons' sentence is sourced to an opened source or cut.

findings.passage: The court record and the victim's later account do not agree, and this profile does not choose between them.
findings.problem: The adverse record is softened and set aside unevenly. Rolling Stone (S10, opened) reports that in October 2001 'Jay-Z admitted to the stabbing and changed his plea to guilty.' The draft drops 'admitted to the stabbing' and frames the dispute as court record against victim, when his own plea and his own memoir ('a mindless assault') are on one side and only Rivera's 2023 statement is on the other. The heading 'The record he does not narrate' is contradicted by the Decoded passage the draft quotes. The handling is also asymmetric. Jay-Z's own account of shooting his brother is used as evidence of protection, while an admitted assault over bootlegged copies of his own album is excluded from type evidence. That incident bears directly on both the 'protecting his work' thesis and the anger-versus-protection question (see critic-F1).
findings.acceptance_test: The section reports that, per Rolling Stone, he admitted the stabbing when he pleaded guilty, and states the plea charge if a source supports it. The heading no longer says he does not narrate it. The article either applies the same rule to both violent incidents or briefly says what the admitted assault does and does not show about the protection-vs-rage reading.

findings.passage: He let West talk about him "100 times," then went silent when West named his wife.
findings.problem: The sequence implied here is not supported. West's November 19, 2016 speech (S14) already complains 'You still ain't calling me,' so Jay-Z's silence was the backdrop to the speech, not shown to begin when Beyonce was named. In the Rap Radar passage (S5, via The Fader) he says the family remark made it 'a real problem,' not that it started a silence. The same Fader passage also has him say 'what really hurt me was, you can't bring my kids and my wife into it,' an admission of hurt that bears on the armor thesis and is not reported.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence matches the sourced sequence: West complained about the silence in the same speech in which he named Beyonce, and Jay-Z later said the family remark made it a real problem. Optionally, the 'what really hurt me' wording is reported if it serves the argument.

protected_passages.passage: The stage on his terms or not at all. The question this profile tries to answer is what that pattern protects: an image, or something he counts as his.
protected_passages.reason: A clean, specific framing that puts the Three-versus-Eight question to the reader before the argument starts. It doesn't presume the answer.

protected_passages.passage: The 2019 NFL deal is the strongest case against this. Partnering with the league while Kaepernick was still out of it drew public criticism from Reid, and telling reporters "we've moved past kneeling" looks more like a Three choosing the bigger platform than an Eight refusing to bend. An Eight reading can say that he chose a seat with power over a gesture, but that is an interpretation, and it should be held loosely.
protected_passages.reason: Honest confrontation of the strongest adverse fact, with the rescue labeled as interpretation. This is the standard the rest of the discriminator should meet.

protected_passages.passage: One possible answer, offered as interpretation rather than proof, is that he learned early that showing feeling was exposure, so his control runs through ownership, terms and timing rather than volume. The answer fits, but it is also convenient, and a reader can reasonably weigh the quiet more heavily than this profile does.
protected_passages.reason: Rare, candid admission that the article's own rescue is convenient. It invites the reader to disagree, which builds trust.

protected_passages.passage: On the Eight reading, nothing changed but who sets the terms. On the Three reading, he waited until the moment would look best. The record available on November 6, 2026 cannot separate the two.
protected_passages.reason: Treats the newest event as not deciding the case, and dates the limitation. It is a strong durability move and an honest one.

protected_passages.passage: He has spent his career refusing to let a label, a league or an audition decide the terms of his work. The one group he names as free to decide is his children.
protected_passages.reason: A distinctive, sourced ending that lands on a specific detail (S9) rather than a thesis restatement. Keep it, but note that the preceding 'turns up again' link from the age-11 promise to the masters is the author's echo, not his, and should read as one.

assessment: The draft is unusually willing to name its weak points: the evidence note, the NFL paragraph, the 'convenient' admission about his quietness, and the undecided 2026 reversal. The problem for a skeptic is the 'What separates them' section, where the article stops grading its own evidence fairly. The protection-over-image discriminator rests on three moves the sources do not support as written. The first recasts an admitted 'Yes' to anger as 'protection rather than rage' (F1). The second is 'each time' and 'never' claims that the draft's own quotes about billing, accolades and bravado contradict (F2, F3). The third counts negotiated wins as costly choices while scoring the one clearly costly, approval-losing move (NFL) only for the rival type (F5). Dash's hostile testimony is converted from 'for money' into evidence of control (F6), and the admitted stabbing is softened and excluded while the brother shooting is used (F7). The bigger gap is the untested counterphobic Six. The draft's wall language (being let down by a trusted figure, danger, toughness covering fear, a loyalty code) fits Six at least as well as Eight, so medium confidence in Eight over Three does not yet beat the strongest real rival (F4). Sources reopened for this review: theGrio 2019 (S7), the Oprah transcript (S1, via r.jina.ai), Rolling Stone 2001 (S10), The Fader 2017 (S5) and Okayplayer 2022 (S13). The quoted passages match except as noted above. T Magazine (S4) and Decoded (S21) remain unopened, as the draft discloses. The similarity advisory tripped only on the shared phrase 'the Eight read(ing)' with Nara-Smith (0.058). That is ordinary type vocabulary with different arguments, not formulaic reuse, so it is not reported as a finding. Risk flags are kept: the Rivera and Buzbee material is sensitive, and the typing is contested (8/3, with 6 untested).
